strengths: AugSub provides a simple, useful training modification: shared parameters and detached prediction targets enable stronger regularization without adding inference cost. Its application to dropout, stochastic depth, and masking gives the framework practical breadth.

The central accuracy gains are well supported. Table A.2 reports ViT-B improving from 83.46±0.04% to 84.08±0.02% with AugMask. Table 3 shows improvements across ViT-S through ViT-H and both 400- and 800-epoch schedules, supporting benefits beyond one architecture or training duration.

The paper explicitly accounts for additional training computation. In Table 6, ViT-B with AugMask achieves 84.1% using 25 GPU-days versus 83.7% using 26 GPU-days for extended baseline training. These comparisons strengthen the practical contribution.

Evaluation extends substantially beyond ImageNet accuracy, covering several pretraining and fine-tuning recipes, hierarchical architectures, robustness, segmentation, detection, and transfer learning. Examples include ImageNet-A improving from 51.9% to 58.3% for ViT-H and ADE20K single-scale mIoU improving from 48.8 to 49.4 for ViT-B.

The pseudocode, detailed recipes in Appendix B, repeated runs for several central experiments, and supplied code link support reproducibility. Together, the empirical breadth and demonstrated utility provide a stronger case for acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: Originality is incremental and insufficiently differentiated experimentally. The objective combines supervised learning with familiar one-way, stop-gradient consistency training. Section 2 acknowledges closely related Co-sub, but no direct comparison establishes the advantage of the proposed asymmetric construction over existing sub-model training.

The ablations do not isolate the claimed benefit of relaxed supervision. Table 1 compares single-pass supervised regularization with a two-pass method that also changes the targets. A control supervising both ordinary and dropped passes with labels, together with a symmetric consistency control, would help establish which design choices explain the gains.

The mechanism claims exceed the evidence. Section 3.1 says regularization is applied exclusively to successfully predicted examples, although Equation 3 contains no correctness gate and can reinforce confident errors. Stop-gradient blocks differentiation through the target, but both passes update shared parameters. Figure 3's aggregate gradient norms support an empirical training trend, not a guarantee of selective regularization or preserved convergence.

The plug-in benefits have meaningful exceptions. Table 10 shows ViT-B CIFAR-100 accuracy falling from 91.9% to 89.6% when AugMask is also used during fine-tuning. Section 4.2 acknowledges unchanged best-checkpoint CLIP accuracy. Training overhead is approximately 1.5× for token-dropping ViTs and 2× for hierarchical architectures, so usefulness remains dependent on the setting.

Statistical support is uneven. Several gains are only 0.1 percentage points, including BEiT v2 and Swin-T, while detection improves by 0.2 box AP; these experiments lack reported repeated-run uncertainty. Appendix A's assertion that transfer gains surpass the standard deviations also does not hold uniformly, such as ViT-S Flowers with AugMask pretraining alone. This limits claims of consistently significant improvement.
